title: Where words turn back: the knower who fears nothing
theme: The vallī closes with its verse: words and mind turn back from Brahman’s bliss, and one who knows it fears nothing; neither the good left undone nor the wrong done torments him.

words.role: relative adverb: the point from which words turn back
words.context: Śaṅkara: «यतः यस्मात् निर्विकल्पात् यथोक्तलक्षणात् अद्वयानन्दात् आत्मनः»
Śaṅkara: names, words («वाचः अभिधानानि»); Bhāradvāja: the Vedas indicated by them («तदुपलक्षितवेदाः»)

words.role: main verb; its subject is the thought quoted in the next two lines
closes the quoted thought, the subject of na tapati

words.meaning: these two (the good and the evil)
words.role: object, construed differently by the commentators (ambiguities)
subject of a verbless sentence: ‘thus [ends] the secret teaching’

sandhi.rule: The visarga (ru) becomes u before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u → o.

sandhi.type: final m before a consonant; aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: ānandam → ānandaṃ, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः); brahmaṇaḥ before v → brahmaṇo, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
a + i → e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). kutaścana is itself kutaḥ + cana with ś for the visarga before c.
na + akaravam: a + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). The base file prints a space after nā; Śaṅkara’s gloss writes the words together («नाकरवं न कृतवानस्मि»).
A final m before a vowel is written together with it.
ete is a dual ending in e and so pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्); it stands unchanged before a vowel, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).
hi + eva → hy eva, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि); eva + eṣaḥ → evaiṣa, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि); eṣaḥ before the vowel of ete loses its visarga.

sandhi_exceptions.note: ete ātmānam: the dual ete is pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्), and does not combine with the following vowel, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).
ete ātmānam again: pragṛhya dual, as in the line before.

morphology.note: Imperfect 1st singular of kṛ, ‘to do’ (a-kar-a-vam): ‘I did’. With na and kim: ‘why did I not do …?’.
Present of bhī, ‘to fear’, a reduplicating root (third class): bi-bhe-ti. In the same verse at 2.4 the text has kadācana, ‘ever’; here kutaścana, ‘from anywhere’.
Present middle of spṛ, a root of the fifth (nu) class: spṛ-ṇu-te. The commentators gloss it ‘pleases, strengthens’ (Śaṅkara: «प्रीणाति बलयति वा») or ‘protects’ (Kūranārāyaṇa: «रक्षति»).
Perfect of vid with present meaning, ‘knows’ (the old perfect-present).

translation.literal: ‘From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having reached [it] — knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing at all.’ This [thought] indeed does not torment him: ‘Why did I not do the good? Why did I do the evil?’ He who knows thus [makes] these two the self (spṛṇute); for he [makes] both of these the self — he who knows thus. Thus the secret teaching (upaniṣad).
translation.readable: ‘Words turn back from it, and the mind with them, without reaching it. Whoever knows that bliss of Brahman fears nothing.’ Such a person is not tormented by the thoughts, ‘Why did I not do the good? Why did I do wrong?’ Knowing this, he holds both the good and the bad within the Self and is strengthened by it — whoever knows thus. This is the secret teaching.

anvaya: यतः वाचः मनसा सह [तत्] अप्राप्य निवर्तन्ते, [तत्] ब्रह्मणः आनन्दम् विद्वान् कुतश्चन न बिभेति इति । एतम् ह वाव ‘किम् अहम् साधु न अकरवम्, किम् अहम् पापम् अकरवम्’ इति न तपति । यः एवम् विद्वान्, सः एते आत्मानम् स्पृणुते । यः एवम् वेद, एषः हि उभे एव एते आत्मानम् स्पृणुते । इति उपनिषत् ।
syntax: The verse is one sentence: a relative clause (yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha) whose antecedent is the bliss of Brahman, then the main clause ‘ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān na bibheti kutaścana’, closed by iti. The prose comments on ‘fears nothing’: a negative main clause (etaṃ ha vāva na tapati) whose subject is the quoted double question (kim ahaṃ … iti). Then a relative–correlative sentence (sa ya evaṃ vidvān … spṛṇute), repeated with hi (‘for’) and a final relative clause (ya evaṃ veda), and the closing formula iti upaniṣat.

ambiguities.topic: Why do words and mind turn back?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: because Brahman, being without distinctions, is not the object of any word or idea; words used to reveal it return having failed to illumine it («अप्राप्य अप्रकाश्यैव निवर्तन्ते»). Kūranārāyaṇa rejects reading this as proof that Brahman is without attributes («कश्चिदाह वाङ्मनसोः निवृत्तिवचनेन निर्विशेषत्वं प्रतिपाद्यते इति । तदसङ्गतम्»): words turn back because the bliss has no limit to reach («तस्य इयत्तायाः अभावादेव वाङ्मनसोः तत्र निवृत्तिः उच्यते»). Bhāradvāja and Gopālānanda gloss the same: what is not reached is the far shore, the limit (Bhāradvāja: «आनन्दस्य इयत्तालक्षणं पारम् अवगन्तुं प्रवृत्ते वाङ्मनसी तदप्राप्य निवृत्ते भवतः»).

Śaṅkara: the knower sees the two, merit and demerit, as the Self, and so ‘strengthens’ the Self (and they lose their power to bind) («परमात्मभावेन उभे पश्यतीत्यर्थः»). Kūranārāyaṇa construes ete as ‘from these two’ and spṛṇute as ‘protects’: he protects himself from both («एते एताभ्याम् आत्मानं स्पृणुते रक्षति»). Gopālānanda: knowing that doing or not doing them brings him neither gain nor loss, he protects himself. The grammar allows both: ete is accusative dual, and the second construction supplies a sense the case does not state.

Śaṅkara takes kim as ‘why’ («किं कस्मात्»): the remorse ‘why did I not do good?’ at the approach of death. Bhāradvāja’s gloss can also be read as ‘what good did I fail to do?’ («साधु - पुण्यकार्यं किमपि नाकरवम्»).

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Lines 1–4 are the anuṣṭubh verse announced at the end of 2.8 (8 + 8 + 8 syllables, and 9 in the fourth line as written, because the quotation mark iti is joined to kutaścana: without it, 8). The rest is prose. The same verse, with kadācana for kutaścana, is quoted at 2.4.

beginner: The vallī ends with a short verse and a comment on it. The verse says that words and thoughts cannot reach Brahman’s bliss: they set out and come back without arriving. But whoever knows that bliss is afraid of nothing. The prose then names the fear that is hardest to escape — looking back on one’s life and asking, ‘Why did I not do the good I could have done? Why did I do that wrong?’ The knower is not tormented by such questions. Śaṅkara says this is because he sees both the good and the bad as no longer his own burden; others say he is protected from both. Either way, the regret that haunts people at the end of life does not touch him. The last words, ‘this is the Upaniṣad’, mark this as the secret at the heart of the teaching.
analogy: Like trying to measure the sky with a ladder: however long the ladder, it comes back down; yet the person who has simply looked up is not troubled by the ladder’s failure.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A verse: ‘From which words turn back with the mind, not having reached — knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing at all.’ Then prose: this does not torment him — ‘Why did I not do the good? Why did I do evil?’ He who knows thus ‘spṛṇute’ the self with these two; for he does so with both — he who knows thus. ‘Thus the Upaniṣad.’

commentary.q: What is it that words cannot reach?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: words and ideas apply to things with distinctions; used of the distinctionless Brahman they turn back without illumining it, and the mind with them, since speech goes only where an idea goes («तस्मात् सहैव वाङ्मनसयोः अभिधानप्रत्ययोः प्रवृत्तिः सर्वत्र»). Kūranārāyaṇa argues against this: if words could not reach Brahman, the whole vallī that describes it would be meaningless, and the verse itself names it ‘bliss’ and ‘of Brahman’ («तदसङ्गतम्»); what words cannot reach is the measure of a bliss that has no measure. Rāmānanda and Gopālānanda gloss alike: the far shore, its extent, is not reached («अप्राप्य इयत्तालक्षणं पारम् अलब्ध्वा»).

commentary.q: Why is the verse repeated from 2.4, with one word changed?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: At 2.4 the verse ends ‘na bibheti kadācana’, ‘never fears’; here ‘kutaścana’, ‘from anywhere’. Śaṅkara notices the difference: at the self made of mind the verse praised the mind by ascribing Brahman to it and denied fear only; here, in the non-dual, the very cause of fear is denied («इह अद्वैतविषये न बिभेति कुतश्चनेति भयनिमित्तमेव प्रतिषिध्यते»), since for the knower there is no second thing to fear («न हि तस्माद्विदुषः अन्यद्वस्त्वन्तरमस्ति भिन्नं यतो बिभेति»).

commentary.q: Why does neither the good undone nor the evil done torment him?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara places the torment at the approach of death: regret for good not done and fear of hell for evil done («पश्चात्सन्तापो भवति आसन्ने मरणकाले»); they torment the ignorant, not the knower. Rāmānanda, Bhāradvāja and Gopālānanda give two reasons: the knower does not desire heaven, and his sins are burnt by knowledge («स्वर्गादिफलेच्छाभावात्», «ब्रह्मज्ञानदग्धसर्वपाप्मत्वाच»). Kūranārāyaṇa compares the Chāndogya: sin does not cling to the knower, as water to a lotus leaf («पुष्करपलाश आपः»).

commentary.q: What does ‘he spṛṇute the self with these two’ mean?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara the knower sees merit and demerit as the Self, emptied of their separate form, and so they become powerless to start another birth («तस्य आत्मभावेन दृष्टे पुण्यपापे निर्वीर्ये अतापके जन्मान्तरारम्भके न भवतः»). For Kūranārāyaṇa he protects himself from the experience of their fruits («पुण्यपापफलानुभवभयात् रक्ष्यति इत्युक्तेः फलानुभवः नास्ति इत्युक्तं भवति»). Both read the repetition as emphasis; Kūranārāyaṇa and Bhāradvāja add that it marks the end of the anuvāka.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the knowledge of Brahman taught in this vallī is the upaniṣad, the highest secret of all knowledge, because the highest good rests in it («सर्वाभ्यः विद्याभ्यः परमरहस्यं दर्शितमित्यर्थः - परं श्रेयः अस्यां निषण्णमिति»). Kūranārāyaṇa: such a secret is not to be told to just anyone, and he cites the Gītā’s warning not to teach it to one without austerity or devotion («इदं ते नातपस्काय नाभक्ताय कदाचन», as cited by him).

advaita.text: Brahman is beyond words because it is without distinctions; the knower fears nothing because nothing exists apart from him to be feared, ignorance having been removed like the second moon seen by a defective eye («तैमिरिकदृष्टद्वितीयचन्द्रवत्»). Merit and demerit, seen as the Self, lose the power to cause another birth.

visistadvaita.text: Words do not fail because Brahman lacks qualities; they fail because its bliss has no limit («तस्य इयत्तायाः अभावादेव वाङ्मनसोः तत्र निवृत्तिः उच्यते»). The meditator who knows that boundless bliss is freed from all fear; he does not desire heaven, his sins are burnt, and he is protected from the fruits of merit and demerit.

dvaita.ref: Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya, at the end of his section on 2.7; no comment on 2.9 in the digital text
dvaita.text: Madhva has no comment on this anuvāka in the imported text. On fear, his verses at 2.7 say that Brahman causes fear to the ignorant and some fear to the knower until he is released («विदुषोऽल्पभयं कुर्याद् यावन्मुक्तिं व्रजत्यसौ»), and for the released Brahman is always fearless («अथाभयं भवेद् ब्रह्म तस्य मुक्तस्य सर्वदा»). How he read ‘yato vāco nivartante’ here is not recorded.

schools.disagreement: All agree that the knower fears nothing and is not tormented by past deeds. They differ on why words turn back — for Śaṅkara because Brahman is without distinctions, for the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators because its bliss has no measure — and on what freedom from merit and demerit means: seeing them as the Self (Śaṅkara), or being protected from their fruits.

parallels.quote: यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते । अप्राप्य मनसा सह
parallels.note: The same verse at the self made of mind, ending ‘na bibheti kadācana’; Śaṅkara explains the change.

parallels.quote: न तत्र चक्षुर्गच्छति न वाग्गच्छति नो मनः
parallels.note: The Kena’s statement that neither eye, speech nor mind goes there.

parallels.quote: एतमु हैवैते न तरत इत्यतः पापमकरवमित्यतः कल्याणमकरवमित्युभे उ हैवैष एते तरति नैनं कृताकृते तपतः
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka has the same thought and the same words (ete, tapataḥ): the knower crosses both ‘I did evil’ and ‘I did good’; what was done and not done does not torment him.

parallels.quote: यथा पुष्करपलाश आपो न श्लिष्यन्त एवमेवंविदि पापं कर्म न श्लिष्यत इति
parallels.note: Cited by Kūranārāyaṇa: evil action does not cling to the knower, as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.

contemporary.text: People who care for the dying often say that the hardest pain at the end is not physical but regret: the things not done, the things done wrongly. The Upaniṣad names exactly these two questions and says that for the knower they lose their sting. It does not say that conduct does not matter — the Śīkṣāvallī ended with a code of conduct — but that what one is matters more than the ledger of what one did. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Is there a ‘why did I not …?’ or ‘why did I …?’ that you carry with you?
reflect.deeper: Words turn back from Brahman, the text says, yet the whole vallī has been describing it. What can words do with something they cannot reach?
reflect.practice: Sit quietly and let one regret come to mind. Notice it without arguing with it, and notice what in you is aware of it.

references.text: Madhva’s bhāṣya as imported has no comment on this anuvāka; his verses on fear at 2.7 are reported as his broader position.

In the six-commentary edition the closing passages of the Ānandavallī run several commentaries together; the importer separates them at their sigla and colophons («इति आनन्दवल्ली कूरनारायणभाष्यम्», «इति आनन्दवल्ली आनन्दभाष्यम्», «इति आनन्दवल्ली प्रतिपदार्थदीपिका»), so each quotation here is from the commentator its colophon names.

The Bhāradvāja file for 2.9 holds his Pratipadārthadīpikā up to its colophon («इति आनन्दवल्ली प्रतिपदार्थदीपिका») and then further, separately marked comments; only the first part is quoted here as Bhāradvāja’s.

flags.note: The base file prints ‘nā karavam’ with a space; the letters are those of na akaravam, as Śaṅkara’s gloss writes it, and the space is removed as a logged spacing correction (corrections.json). Madhva’s text spells the anusvāra before sibilants as ग्ं (spelling only).
The construction of ‘ete ātmānaṃ spṛṇute’ is disputed: ‘makes these two the Self / strengthens the Self’ (Śaṅkara) or ‘protects himself from these two’ (Kūranārāyaṇa).
The six-commentary text for 2.9 runs several commentaries together across its colophons; the importer now splits them there. The OCR text should still be read against the printed book.
